42	WEEK 6 ASSIGNMENTSEMESTER API · PART 1 OF 2
43	Semester API, Part 1: Design and Build Your API
44	This week you build the API your mobile app will talk to for the rest of the semester. It stores data in a JSON file, uses the same five layers as the speedrun leaderboard, and ships with a Postman collection that proves every endpoint works, including the ones that are supposed to fail.
45	1What You're Building
46	You're building the back end for your own semester app, not the leaderboard. Everything in the Week 6 pages applies directly: swap "runs" for your resource and follow the same structure. If you get stuck, find the matching section in the pages and compare your code to the leaderboard's.
47	Part 1 is JSON file storage only. Part 2 next week adds SQL Server in Docker, a configuration flag to switch between the two, and logging. If you build Part 1 the way the pages show, Part 2 is a new repository class and one changed line in `Program.cs`. If you take shortcuts here, Part 2 turns into a rewrite.
48	You don't touch the MAUI app this week or next. The app starts calling your API once the API is finished.
49	2Pick Your Primary Resource
50	Your app probably has several kinds of data. For Part 1, pick one primary resource, the thing your app is mostly about, and build it completely. A finished resource with every layer, rule, and test beats three half-built ones. Here's what that looks like for the most common project types:
51	Recipe Collection
52	Primary: `/api/recipes`: name, ingredients, instructions, image URL, prep minutes.
53	Business rule idea: no two recipes with the same name (409).
54	Later: categories, favorites
55	Personal Finance
56	Primary: `/api/transactions`: date, amount, category, description.
57	Business rule idea: no duplicate transaction with the same date, amount, and description (409).
58	Later: budget categories, goals
59	Fitness Tracker
60	Primary: `/api/workouts`: date, type, duration minutes, calories burned.
61	Business rule idea: only one workout of the same type per day (409).
62	Later: meals, progress metrics
63	Your project is something else? Good. Apply the same pattern: one resource, full CRUD, and one business rule that depends on existing data. If you're not sure which resource is "primary," ask me before you start building.
64	3Requirements
65	Each group below maps to a Week 6 page. Every box is something I check when grading.
66	A. Design firstPage 1
67	
68	* Your repository has a `README.md` with an endpoint table: method, URL, what it does, success code, and failure codes, in the same format as the leaderboard table.
69	* The endpoint table is committed before your controller exists. I'll check the commit history.
70	* URLs use plural nouns and no verbs: `/api/recipes/{id}`, not `/api/getRecipe`.
71	
72	B. Project and layersPage 2
73	
74	* ASP.NET Core Web API on .NET 10, with controllers and OpenAPI enabled. .NET 8 and 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026, mid-semester, so they aren't accepted.
75	* The WeatherForecast sample files are deleted.
76	* Folders: `Controllers`, `DTOs`, `Models`, `Repositories`, `Services`, `Data`.
77	* A Model with at least one field the client can't set, such as an id, a created date, or a server-controlled flag.
78	* Separate request and response DTOs. The controller never accepts or returns the Model.
79	* Interfaces for both the service and the repository. The service depends on the repository interface, and the controller depends on the service interface.
80	* At least one business rule in the service that depends on existing data (a duplicate check or similar), reported to the controller as an outcome, not an HTTP code.
81	* DI registrations in `Program.cs`: repository as a singleton, service as scoped.
82	
83	C. JSON file repositoryPage 3
84	
85	* Data lives in `Data/<resource>.json` under the content root.
86	* Every public method that touches the file is guarded by one `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)`, with `WaitAsync` above the `try` and `Release` in the `finally`.
87	* Writes go to a temp file first, then `File.Move(..., overwrite: true)`.
88	* A missing or empty file is treated as an empty list, not a crash.
89	* Ids are assigned by the repository, inside the guarded section.
90	* Every method is async and takes a `CancellationToken`.
91	
92	D. Controller, validation, and errorsPage 4
93	
94	* `[ApiController]` with a literal route (`[Route("api/recipes")]`) and `:int` constraints on id routes.
95	* GET all, GET by id, POST, PUT, DELETE, plus at least one query-string filter on GET all.
96	* Correct status codes: 200, 201 via `CreatedAtAction` (with a `Location` header), 204, 400, 404, and 409 for your business rule.
97	* Actions stay thin: call the service once, then map the result. No file access, no business rules.
98	* At least four validation rules on the request DTO using DataAnnotations, with your own error messages. Use explicit `[Required]` on strings.
99	* Validation error keys use JSON names (`SystemTextJsonValidationMetadataProvider`).
100	* `AddProblemDetails()` and `UseExceptionHandler()` in `Program.cs`.
101	* Don't wrap every action in `try/catch`. The exception handler covers unexpected errors in one place. Catching an exception and returning 200, or returning a 500 you built by hand, loses points.
102	
103	E. Postman collectionPage 5
104	
105	* Built from your API's OpenAPI document, with `{{baseUrl}}` and an id variable set from the POST response.
106	* At least one request for every endpoint, plus at least one failure request for every endpoint that can fail (400, 404, 409).
107	* Every request has at least one `pm.test` on the status code. POST also checks the `Location` header and that over-posting is ignored.
108	* The collection cleans up after itself and passes twice in a row in the Collection Runner.
109	* Exported to a `postman/` folder in your repository.
110	
111	F. Git
112	
113	* `Data/*.json` test data and `Data/*.tmp` are in `.gitignore`. If you want starting data, commit a separate seed file.
114	* Commits throughout the week with messages that say what changed. One giant commit on the due date loses points.
115	
116	4What to Submit
117	
118	1. Your GitHub repository link. Make sure I have access.
119	2. A video, 5 minutes or less, that shows these in order:
120	   1. Your endpoint table in the README.
121	   2. The folder structure in Visual Studio, and the DI registrations in `Program.cs`.
122	   3. Your full Postman collection running in the Collection Runner, all green.
123	   4. One POST in Postman, then `Data/<resource>.json` opened to show the new record, including a field the client couldn't set.
124	   5. One validation failure, with the error body on screen, and one 409 from your business rule.
125	   6. Thirty seconds on one thing that broke while you built this and how you found it.
126	
127	Coming in Part 2 (Week 7)
128	You'll run SQL Server in a Docker container locally, write a second repository that implements the same interface against it, and add a setting in `appsettings.json` that switches between JSON and SQL Server storage without changing any other layer. You'll also add structured logging. Your Part 1 Postman collection should pass unchanged against the SQL Server version. That's the test that proves your layers are separated.

WEEK 6 ASSIGNMENTSEMESTER API · PART 1 OF 2
Semester API, Part 1: Design and Build Your API
This week you build the API your mobile app will talk to for the rest of the semester. It stores data in a JSON file, uses the same five layers as the speedrun leaderboard, and ships with a Postman collection that proves every endpoint works, including the ones that are supposed to fail.
1What You're Building
You're building the back end for your own semester app, not the leaderboard. Everything in the Week 6 pages applies directly: swap "runs" for your resource and follow the same structure. If you get stuck, find the matching section in the pages and compare your code to the leaderboard's.
Part 1 is JSON file storage only. Part 2 next week adds SQL Server in Docker, a configuration flag to switch between the two, and logging. If you build Part 1 the way the pages show, Part 2 is a new repository class and one changed line in `Program.cs`. If you take shortcuts here, Part 2 turns into a rewrite.
You don't touch the MAUI app this week or next. The app starts calling your API once the API is finished.
2Pick Your Primary Resource
Your app probably has several kinds of data. For Part 1, pick one primary resource, the thing your app is mostly about, and build it completely. A finished resource with every layer, rule, and test beats three half-built ones. Here's what that looks like for the most common project types:
Recipe Collection
Primary: `/api/recipes`: name, ingredients, instructions, image URL, prep minutes.
Business rule idea: no two recipes with the same name (409).
Later: categories, favorites
Personal Finance
Primary: `/api/transactions`: date, amount, category, description.
Business rule idea: no duplicate transaction with the same date, amount, and description (409).
Later: budget categories, goals
Fitness Tracker
Primary: `/api/workouts`: date, type, duration minutes, calories burned.
Business rule idea: only one workout of the same type per day (409).
Later: meals, progress metrics
Your project is something else? Good. Apply the same pattern: one resource, full CRUD, and one business rule that depends on existing data. If you're not sure which resource is "primary," ask me before you start building.
3Requirements
Each group below maps to a Week 6 page. Every box is something I check when grading.
A. Design firstPage 1

* Your repository has a `README.md` with an endpoint table: method, URL, what it does, success code, and failure codes, in the same format as the leaderboard table.
* The endpoint table is committed before your controller exists. I'll check the commit history.
* URLs use plural nouns and no verbs: `/api/recipes/{id}`, not `/api/getRecipe`.

B. Project and layersPage 2

* ASP.NET Core Web API on .NET 10, with controllers and OpenAPI enabled. .NET 8 and 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026, mid-semester, so they aren't accepted.
* The WeatherForecast sample files are deleted.
* Folders: `Controllers`, `DTOs`, `Models`, `Repositories`, `Services`, `Data`.
* A Model with at least one field the client can't set, such as an id, a created date, or a server-controlled flag.
* Separate request and response DTOs. The controller never accepts or returns the Model.
* Interfaces for both the service and the repository. The service depends on the repository interface, and the controller depends on the service interface.
* At least one business rule in the service that depends on existing data (a duplicate check or similar), reported to the controller as an outcome, not an HTTP code.
* DI registrations in `Program.cs`: repository as a singleton, service as scoped.

C. JSON file repositoryPage 3

* Data lives in `Data/<resource>.json` under the content root.
* Every public method that touches the file is guarded by one `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)`, with `WaitAsync` above the `try` and `Release` in the `finally`.
* Writes go to a temp file first, then `File.Move(..., overwrite: true)`.
* A missing or empty file is treated as an empty list, not a crash.
* Ids are assigned by the repository, inside the guarded section.
* Every method is async and takes a `CancellationToken`.

D. Controller, validation, and errorsPage 4

* `[ApiController]` with a literal route (`[Route("api/recipes")]`) and `:int` constraints on id routes.
* GET all, GET by id, POST, PUT, DELETE, plus at least one query-string filter on GET all.
* Correct status codes: 200, 201 via `CreatedAtAction` (with a `Location` header), 204, 400, 404, and 409 for your business rule.
* Actions stay thin: call the service once, then map the result. No file access, no business rules.
* At least four validation rules on the request DTO using DataAnnotations, with your own error messages. Use explicit `[Required]` on strings.
* Validation error keys use JSON names (`SystemTextJsonValidationMetadataProvider`).
* `AddProblemDetails()` and `UseExceptionHandler()` in `Program.cs`.
* Don't wrap every action in `try/catch`. The exception handler covers unexpected errors in one place. Catching an exception and returning 200, or returning a 500 you built by hand, loses points.

E. Postman collectionPage 5

* Built from your API's OpenAPI document, with `{{baseUrl}}` and an id variable set from the POST response.
* At least one request for every endpoint, plus at least one failure request for every endpoint that can fail (400, 404, 409).
* Every request has at least one `pm.test` on the status code. POST also checks the `Location` header and that over-posting is ignored.
* The collection cleans up after itself and passes twice in a row in the Collection Runner.
* Exported to a `postman/` folder in your repository.

F. Git

* `Data/*.json` test data and `Data/*.tmp` are in `.gitignore`. If you want starting data, commit a separate seed file.
* Commits throughout the week with messages that say what changed. One giant commit on the due date loses points.

4What to Submit

1. Your GitHub repository link. Make sure I have access.
2. A video, 5 minutes or less, that shows these in order:
   1. Your endpoint table in the README.
   2. The folder structure in Visual Studio, and the DI registrations in `Program.cs`.
   3. Your full Postman collection running in the Collection Runner, all green.
   4. One POST in Postman, then `Data/<resource>.json` opened to show the new record, including a field the client couldn't set.
   5. One validation failure, with the error body on screen, and one 409 from your business rule.
   6. Thirty seconds on one thing that broke while you built this and how you found it.

Coming in Part 2 (Week 7)
You'll run SQL Server in a Docker container locally, write a second repository that implements the same interface against it, and add a setting in `appsettings.json` that switches between JSON and SQL Server storage without changing any other layer. You'll also add structured logging. Your Part 1 Postman collection should pass unchanged against the SQL Server version. That's the test that proves your layers are separated.

# GritTrack

## Stack
- **API:** ASP.NET Core Web API (.NET 10), JWT auth, switchable JSON/SQL repository
- **App:** .NET MAUI (Android), MVVM pattern, SecureStorage for tokens
- **Database:** SQL Server in Docker, EF Core migrations
- **Domain:** Course tracking (grades, credits, GPA calculation)

## Code Style
- **No var** - typed declarations only (string, int, bool, the real stuff)
- **Comments with personality** - section headers like CSS blocks, plus inline WHY/WHAT
- **OOP modularly** - reusable logic gets its own controller or modal, injected when needed
- **Repository pattern** - database access behind a data store so we're never married to one SQL flavor

## Project Structure
```
GritTrack.Api/          # ASP.NET Core API
  Controllers/          # Thin, calls service once
  DTOs/                 # Request/Response, never the Model
  Models/               # Domain entities
  Repositories/         # JSON + SQL implementations
  Services/             # Business rules
  Data/                 # DbContext, JSON files

GritTrack/              # MAUI app
  PageModels/           # ViewModels (MVVM)
  Pages/                # XAML views
  Services/             # API client, auth, navigation
```

## Running It
1. `docker compose up -d` (SQL Server)
2. API: `dotnet run` in GritTrack.Api (needs User Secrets for Auth:SigningKey, Auth:DemoPassword, Database:Password)
3. App: Run GritTrack project targeting Android emulator

## Credentials
- Demo login: `demo` / password in User Secrets (Auth:DemoPassword)
- appsettings.json has `Auth:Enabled` and `DataSource` (Json|SqlServer)

35	    // get all courses, optionally filter by grade letter
36	    public async Task<List<Course>> GetCoursesAsync(string? grade, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
37	    {
38	        List<Course> courses = await _repository.GetAllAsync(cancellationToken);
39	
40	        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(grade))
41	        {
42	            courses = courses
43	                .Where(course => string.Equals(course.CurrentGrade, grade, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
44	                .ToList();
45	        }
46	
47	        return courses;

55	    public async Task<(SaveCourseOutcome Outcome, Course? Course)> CreateCourseAsync(CourseRequestDto request, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
56	    {
57	        // no two courses can have the same code - that's our uniqueness rule
58	        // trim first, because " CS201 " gets saved as "CS201" and would sneak past the check
59	        Course? existing = await _repository.GetByCourseCodeAsync(request.CourseCode.Trim(), cancellationToken);
60	        if (existing is not null)
61	            return (SaveCourseOutcome.DuplicateCourseCode, null);
62	
63	        Course course = new Course
64	        {
65	            Name = request.Name.Trim(),
66	            CourseCode = request.CourseCode.Trim(),
67	            Instructor = request.Instructor?.Trim(),
68	            Credits = request.Credits,

14	    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _fileLock = new(1, 1);
15	
16	    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions SerializerOptions = new()
17	    {
18	        WriteIndented = true
19	    };

21	    public JsonCourseRepository(IWebHostEnvironment environment)
22	    {
23	        string dataFolder = Path.Combine(environment.ContentRootPath, "Data");
24	        Directory.CreateDirectory(dataFolder);

28	    /// <inheritdoc />

30	    {

32	        try
33	        {
34	            return await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
35	        }
36	        finally
37	        {
38	            _fileLock.Release();
39	        }
40	    }
41	
42	    /// <inheritdoc />
43	    public async Task<Course?> GetByIdAsync(int id, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
44	    {
45	        await _fileLock.WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
46	        try
47	        {
48	            List<Course> courses = await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
49	            return courses.FirstOrDefault(course => course.Id == id);
50	        }
51	        finally
52	        {
53	            _fileLock.Release();
54	        }
55	    }
56	
57	    /// <inheritdoc />
58	    public async Task<Course?> GetByCourseCodeAsync(string courseCode, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
59	    {
60	        await _fileLock.WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
61	        try
62	        {
63	            List<Course> courses = await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
64	            return courses.FirstOrDefault(course =>
65	                string.Equals(course.CourseCode, courseCode, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
66	        }
67	        finally
68	        {
69	            _fileLock.Release();
70	        }
71	    }
72	
73	    /// <inheritdoc />
74	    public async Task<Course> AddAsync(Course course, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
75	    {
76	        await _fileLock.WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
77	        try
78	        {
79	            List<Course> courses = await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
80	            course.Id = courses.Count == 0 ? 1 : courses.Max(existing => existing.Id) + 1;
81	            courses.Add(course);
82	
83	            await WriteAllAsync(courses, cancellationToken);
84	            return course;
85	        }
86	        finally
87	        {
88	            _fileLock.Release();
89	        }
90	    }

94	    {
95	        await _fileLock.WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
96	        try
97	        {
98	            List<Course> courses = await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
99	            int index = courses.FindIndex(existing => existing.Id == course.Id);
100	            if (index < 0)
101	                return false;
102	
103	            courses[index] = course;
104	            await WriteAllAsync(courses, cancellationToken);
105	            return true;
106	        }
107	        finally

109	            _fileLock.Release();
110	        }
111	    }

114	    public async Task<bool> DeleteAsync(int id, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
115	    {
116	        await _fileLock.WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
117	        try
118	        {
119	            List<Course> courses = await ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
120	            int removed = courses.RemoveAll(course => course.Id == id);
121	            if (removed == 0)
122	                return false;
123	
124	            await WriteAllAsync(courses, cancellationToken);

134	    private async Task<List<Course>> ReadAllAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
135	    {
136	        if (!File.Exists(_filePath))
137	            return new List<Course>();
138	
139	        await using FileStream stream = File.OpenRead(_filePath);
140	        if (stream.Length == 0)
141	            return new List<Course>();
142	
143	        List<Course>? courses = await JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync<List<Course>>(stream, SerializerOptions, cancellationToken);
144	        return courses ?? new List<Course>();

149	    private async Task WriteAllAsync(List<Course> courses, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
150	    {

152	        string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(courses, SerializerOptions);
153	        await File.WriteAllTextAsync(tempPath, json, CancellationToken.None);

3	/// <summary>
4	/// Runs the "apply migrations" step and keeps trying while SQL Server is still waking up.
5	/// Pulled out of Program.cs so the retry rules can be tested without a real database.
6	/// </summary>
7	public static class DatabaseMigrationRunner
8	{
9	    /// <summary>How many times to try before giving up.</summary>
10	    public const int DefaultMaximumAttempts = 6;
11	
12	    /// <summary>How long to wait between tries.</summary>
13	    public static readonly TimeSpan DefaultDelay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);
14	
15	    /// <summary>
16	    /// Runs migrate. If it throws, logs a warning, waits, and tries again. The last attempt does not
17	    /// catch anything, so the real error reaches the caller.
18	    /// </summary>
19	    /// <param name="migrate">The work to try, normally context.Database.MigrateAsync.</param>
20	    /// <param name="logger">Where the "not ready yet" warnings go.</param>
21	    /// <param name="maximumAttempts">Total tries, including the first one.</param>
22	    /// <param name="wait">How to wait between tries. Tests swap this out so they don't sleep for real.</param>
23	    public static async Task RunWithRetryAsync(
24	        Func<Task> migrate,
25	        ILogger logger,
26	        int maximumAttempts = DefaultMaximumAttempts,
27	        Func<TimeSpan, Task>? wait = null)
28	    {
29	        wait ??= delay => Task.Delay(delay);
30	
31	        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
32	        {
33	            try
34	            {
35	                await migrate();
36	                return;
37	            }
38	            catch (Exception exception) when (attempt < maximumAttempts)
39	            {
40	                // only the exception type goes in the log, never its message (it can hold the connection string)
41	                logger.LogWarning("Database not ready yet (attempt {Attempt} of {Maximum}): {Reason}",
42	                    attempt, maximumAttempts, exception.GetType().Name);
43	                await wait(DefaultDelay);
44	            }
45	        }
46	    }
47	}
